name: Gates County

actions.title: One-Year Moratorium on Data Centers and High-Impact Facilities
actions.summary: Gates County commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on all data center and related high-capacity facility development approvals in unincorporated areas, making it the first NC county to do so.

contextBlurb: Gates County, in northeastern North Carolina, was the first county in the state to enact a one-year data center moratorium in December 2025, sparked by two unsolicited inquiries from a firm that promotes data center ordinances. Commissioners acted proactively despite no active project being on file, citing concerns about environmental, infrastructure, and economic impacts on the county's rural character. The moratorium covers all unincorporated areas and directs staff to study impacts and draft permanent regulations.

name: Chatham County

actions.title: 12-Month Moratorium on Data Centers and Cryptocurrency Mining
actions.summary: Chatham County commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on permitting data centers and crypto mining in unincorporated areas, lasting until February 2027 or until new zoning regulations are adopted.

actions.title: Eco TIP West LLC Lawsuit Over 750 MW Project Freeze
actions.summary: Developer Eco TIP West LLC filed suit against Chatham County challenging the moratorium as applied to its frozen 750 MW data center project, arguing vested rights under prior Heavy Industrial zoning.

contextBlurb: Chatham County became the second NC county to halt data center permitting when commissioners unanimously passed a 12-month moratorium in February 2026 following a public hearing with more than two dozen speakers. The moratorium also covers cryptocurrency mining and data processing facilities, and directs planning staff to review environmental impacts, study other jurisdictions' regulations, and develop new zoning standards. The county faces a legal challenge from developer Eco TIP West LLC, whose large project was effectively frozen by the moratorium.

name: Orange County

actions.title: One-Year Moratorium on Large-Scale Data Centers
actions.summary: Orange County commissioners adopted a one-year moratorium on data center development approvals after a public hearing, authorizing staff to evaluate electricity demand, water usage, land-use compatibility, and utility cost impacts.

contextBlurb: Orange County's Board of Commissioners approved a one-year data center moratorium in April 2026 under NCGS 160D-107, following a March 2026 unanimous board direction to evaluate large-scale data center impacts. Staff presented findings on electricity demand, water use, land compatibility, and utility cost effects before the board acted. Nearby jurisdictions including Hillsborough (within Orange County), Durham, Chatham County, and Apex in Wake County have passed similar measures, reflecting the dense cluster of moratoriums around the Research Triangle.

name: Rowan County

actions.title: One-Year Moratorium on New Data Centers
actions.summary: Rowan County commissioners passed a one-year moratorium on new data center permits following intense community opposition to a planned 400-acre Edged Energy facility, though the moratorium explicitly exempts projects already underway.

contextBlurb: Rowan County residents launched a petition and packed local meetings to oppose two proposed data centers, including a 400-acre facility by Edged Energy, citing concerns about noise, heat island effects, and water usage near residential areas. Community activist Mark Ortiz helped organize the opposition, and commissioners responded by enacting a one-year moratorium on new data centers in April 2026, though the already-in-progress Edged Energy site was grandfathered. Meanwhile, the city of Salisbury (the county seat) separately passed a land-development ordinance text amendment allowing data centers with restrictions on maximum size, noise, and water consumption.

name: Stokes County

actions.title: Project Delta Rezoning Approved (3-2 Vote)
actions.summary: Commissioners narrowly approved rezoning 1,844 acres from residential-agricultural to heavy manufacturing for the proposed Project Delta hyperscale data center, overruling the local planning board over overwhelming public opposition.

actions.title: Lawsuit Filed Challenging Project Delta Rezoning
actions.summary: Thirteen residents and four nonprofits, represented by SCSJ and SELC, sued Stokes County alleging the rezoning violated statutory notice requirements and failed to account for environmental and cultural impacts along the Dan River.

actions.title: January Rezoning Voided by Commissioners
actions.summary: Stokes County commissioners voted to formally void the January rezoning approval and related text amendments after acknowledging that public notice for the original hearing did not meet state law requirements, resetting Project Delta to square one.

contextBlurb: Stokes County became a flashpoint in North Carolina's data center debate when commissioners approved a 3-2 rezoning of nearly 1,844 acres near Walnut Cove for the 'Project Delta' hyperscale campus in January 2026, overriding the planning board's recommendation and facing more than 100 protesters inside and outside the hearing chamber. A citizen lawsuit by SCSJ and SELC challenged the approval on procedural grounds, and in April 2026 commissioners voted to void the rezoning entirely after acknowledging it failed to meet state notice requirements. Residents and plaintiffs are now calling for a formal moratorium before any reapplication is considered, citing concerns about the Dan River corridor, Indigenous and historic Black cultural sites, and noise from 24/7 gas generator operations.

name: Clay County

actions.title: One-Year Moratorium on Data Centers
actions.summary: Clay County enacted a one-year moratorium on data center development in September 2025, part of an early wave of bans across western North Carolina mountain communities.

contextBlurb: Clay County, a small mountain county in far western North Carolina, was among the earliest jurisdictions in the state to enact a data center moratorium, passing a one-year ban in September 2025 alongside the city of Brevard. The moratorium reflects broader concerns in Appalachian communities about water resources, grid capacity, and the compatibility of hyperscale industrial facilities with rural mountain character. Clay County's action helped catalyze a wave of similar measures across the western NC region.

name: Town of Apex (Wake County)

actions.title: One-Year Data Center Moratorium
actions.summary: The Apex Town Council unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on data center development to allow time to develop guidelines, following a withdrawn 250 MW proposal near the Shearon Harris Nuclear Plant.

actions.title: Wendell Data Center Moratorium Through December 31, 2026
actions.summary: The Wendell Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to pause new data center permitting applications through the end of 2026, or until updated regulations are in place, despite no active data center proposals in the town.

contextBlurb: Two Wake County municipalities — Apex and Wendell — both enacted data center moratoriums within a day of each other in April 2026, reflecting the Triangle corridor's growing regulatory pushback against AI-driven data center expansion. Apex acted in part following a developer's withdrawal of a 250 MW data center proposal near the Shearon Harris Nuclear Plant, while Wendell passed its freeze proactively with no pending applications. Wake County's Board of Commissioners simultaneously engaged in broader discussions about data center planning and resources in March 2026.

name: Lee County

actions.title: Data Center Definitions and Regulations Added to Unified Development Ordinance
actions.summary: Lee County added specific data center definitions and use regulations to its Unified Development Ordinance in April 2026, choosing to set affirmative standards rather than enact a moratorium.

contextBlurb: Lee County took a regulatory rather than prohibitory approach in April 2026, amending its Unified Development Ordinance to formally define 'data center' as a land use and establish governing standards, joining neighboring Sanford in that same month. This path contrasts with the moratorium approach taken by more than 20 other NC jurisdictions and reflects a willingness to accommodate data centers subject to clear rules. The UDO update gives planners a framework to evaluate future proposals against specific performance criteria without a blanket pause on permitting.
